notes: Original practice questions for Ratio. No official questions are reproduced.
format_note: Topic-focused, no-calculator multiple-choice sets in the current ESAT style. Allow 15 minutes per set.

questions.stem:
A metal has density 2.7 g/cm³.

What is its density in kg/m³?
questions.explanation: A cubic metre contains 10⁶ cm³ and a kilogram contains 10³ g, so 2.7 × 10⁶ ÷ 10³ = 2700 kg/m³. Converting only the mass misses the change in volume unit.

questions.stem: What is 4.2 × 10⁻⁵ + 7.6 × 10⁻⁶ in standard form?
questions.explanation: Write 7.6 × 10⁻⁶ as 0.76 × 10⁻⁵, then add 4.2 and 0.76. Adding the coefficients before matching the powers of ten gives the wrong place values.

questions.stem:
The ratios of red to green and green to blue tiles in a mosaic are 2 : 3 and 4 : 5 respectively. There are 90 blue tiles.

How many red tiles are there?
questions.explanation: Match the green terms at 12 to get red : green : blue = 8 : 12 : 15. Since 15 parts are 90, 8 parts are 48; the ratios cannot be joined without matching their green terms.

questions.stem:
A beacon flashes every 18 seconds and another every 24 seconds. The first flashes at time 0 and the second at time 6 seconds.

At what time do they first flash together?
questions.explanation: The second beacon flashes at 6, 30 and 54 seconds, and 54 is the first of these divisible by 18. The LCM, 72 seconds, is the gap between joint flashes, not the time of the first one.

questions.stem: What is the exact value of 5/√10 − √40/10?
questions.explanation: Rationalising the first term gives √10/2, and √40/10 = √10/5. Subtracting gives 3√10/10; √40 is twice √10, not four times it.

questions.stem:
A runner covers 150 m to the nearest 10 m in 20 s to the nearest second.

What is the greatest lower bound for her average speed in m/s?
questions.explanation: Use the lower distance bound 145 m and the upper time bound 20.5 s: 145 ÷ 20.5 = 290/41. A smaller time would increase speed, so taking both lower bounds does not give the lower speed bound.

questions.stem:
An account pays 10% interest at the end of each year. Immediately after the first interest payment, £110 is withdrawn. Immediately after the second interest payment, the balance is £1089.

What was the opening balance?
questions.explanation: Undo the final interest to get £990, restore the £110 to get £1100, then undo the first interest to get £1000. Adding the withdrawal after undoing both interest payments puts it at the wrong point in the calculation.

questions.stem:
For positive x and z, y is directly proportional to x² and inversely proportional to √z. The value of x increases by 50%.

What must be the ratio of the new value of z to its original value for y to stay unchanged?
questions.explanation: The x² factor grows by (3/2)² = 9/4, so √z must grow by the same factor. Squaring gives 81/16; 9 : 4 is the ratio for √z, not for z.

questions.stem:
Let a = 0.111… and b = 0.090909…, where the blocks 1 and 09 repeat respectively.

What is (a − b) ÷ (a + b)?
questions.explanation: Multiplying by 10 or 100 and subtracting the original decimal gives a = 1/9 and b = 9/99 = 1/11. The difference over the sum is (11 − 9)/(11 + 9) = 1/10; treating b as the terminating 0.09 changes both terms.

questions.stem:
A tank holds a 12% salt solution by mass. One quarter of the solution is drained and replaced with the same mass of water. Then one third of the new solution is drained and replaced with the same mass of 30% salt solution. The tank is mixed thoroughly before each draining.

What is the final percentage of salt by mass?
questions.explanation: After the first replacement the concentration is 12% × 3/4 = 9%. Two thirds of the final mixture is at 9% and one third at 30%, giving 6% + 10% = 16%; the second drain removes salt as well as water.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of x in (2x − 3)(x + 5) − (x − 1)²?
questions.explanation: The first product contributes 10 − 3 = 7, and subtracting the second contributes +2. The minus sign applies to the whole square, not just its first term.

questions.stem:
For positive p and q, v = (p − q)/(p + q).

Which expression equals p in terms of q and v?
questions.explanation: Cross-multiplying gives vp + vq = p − q, so p(1 − v) = q(1 + v). The vq term has the opposite sign from vp after collecting the p and q terms on separate sides.

questions.stem:
A sequence begins at 5. To get each new term, double the previous term and subtract 3.

What is the fourth term?
questions.explanation: The terms are 5, 7, 11, 19. Starting at 5 means only three applications of the rule are needed; a fourth gives 35.

questions.stem: For x ≠ 2 and x ≠ −2, which expression equals 1/(x − 2) − 1/(x + 2)?
questions.explanation: The common denominator is (x − 2)(x + 2) and the numerator is (x + 2) − (x − 2) = 4. Subtracting the denominators instead does not give an equivalent fraction.

questions.stem:
The line through (−3, 4) and (5, −2) crosses the x-axis at (a, 0).

What is a?
questions.explanation: The gradient is −6/8 = −3/4. Dropping from y = 4 to y = 0 needs a horizontal increase of 16/3, so a = −3 + 16/3 = 7/3; the increase is not the coordinate itself.

questions.stem:
The graph y = x² − 6x + k touches the x-axis.

What is the y-coordinate where it crosses the y-axis?
questions.explanation: Write y = (x − 3)² + k − 9. Touching the x-axis means the minimum is zero, so k = 9 and y = 9 when x = 0; the turning-point x-coordinate 3 is not the intercept.

questions.stem: What is the smallest integer x satisfying 7 − 3x < (x + 5)/2?
questions.explanation: Multiplying by 2 and collecting terms gives 9 < 7x. The cutoff is 9/7, not 1, so the smallest integer allowed is 2.

questions.stem:
Let f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = x² − x − 4. There are two values of x for which f(x) = g(x).

What is the product of the two corresponding values of f(x)?
questions.explanation: Equating the expressions for y gives x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0. The y-coordinates are 8 and 2, so their product is 16; −8 is the product of the x-coordinates.

questions.stem:
A sequence has nth term an² + bn + c. Its first three terms are 6, 11 and 20.

What is the first term greater than 100?
questions.explanation: The second difference is 4, so a = 2; the first increase gives b = −1 and the first term gives c = 5. The sequence is increasing, with seventh term 96 and eighth term 125; using the first difference as a constant would miss the quadratic growth.

questions.stem:
A speed–time graph consists of straight segments joining (0, 0), (4, 6), (10, 6) and (14, 2), with time in seconds and speed in m/s.

At what time has half the total distance been travelled?
questions.explanation: The three areas are 12, 36 and 16 m, so halfway is 32 m. After the initial 12 m, another 20 m takes 20/6 s, giving 22/3 s; half the time is not half the distance.

questions.stem:
Two angles of a quadrilateral are 100° and 116°. The other two angles are equal.

What is the size of each of those equal angles?
questions.explanation: The angles left over total 360° − 100° − 116° = 144°. Divide this remainder by two, rather than using the full remaining angle as the answer.

questions.stem:
Point P is at (7, 1). It is enlarged by scale factor −2 about (3, −1).

What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.explanation: The displacement from the centre is (4, 2), which becomes (−8, −4). Add the centre back to get (−5, −5); multiplying P’s coordinates directly would enlarge from the origin.

questions.stem:
The bearing of B from A is 248°.

What is the bearing of A from B?
questions.explanation: The reverse direction differs by 180°, so subtract 180° to get the three-figure bearing 068°. Subtracting 248° from 360° would reflect the direction, not reverse it.

questions.stem:
A sector of radius 9 cm has area 27π/2 cm².

What is its perimeter in cm?
questions.explanation: The area is one sixth of 81π, so the arc length is one sixth of 18π, or 3π. The perimeter also includes both radii, not just the curved edge.

questions.stem:
A straight ramp of length 10 m slopes upwards at 30° to the horizontal. From its upper end a second straight ramp of length 4 m slopes downwards at 45° to the horizontal.

How far above the starting point is the end of the second ramp?
questions.explanation: The first ramp rises 10 sin 30° = 5 m, and the second falls 4 sin 45° = 2√2 m. Subtract the vertical drop; using cos 30° would use the first ramp’s horizontal run.

questions.stem:
A and B are points on a circle with centre O. The minor angle AOB is 140° and C is on the minor arc AB, distinct from A and B.

What is angle ACB?
questions.explanation: C lies on the minor arc, so angle ACB subtends the major arc AB. Its angle at the centre is 360° − 140° = 220°, giving 110° at C rather than half the minor angle.

questions.stem:
From A to B the displacement is (6, −3), and from B to C it is (−4, 5). M is the midpoint of AC.

What is the displacement from B to M?
questions.explanation: From A to C the displacement is (2, 2), so from A to M it is (1, 1). Subtract the displacement from A to B to get (−5, 4); halving AC does not start you at B.

questions.stem:
The sides of triangle ABC satisfy AB = 15 cm and AC = 20 cm. D lies on AB with AD = 9 cm. The line through D parallel to BC meets AC at E. The area of quadrilateral DBCE is 96 cm².

What is the area of triangle ADE?
questions.explanation: The length scale factor is 3/5, so triangle ADE is 9/25 of the whole area and DBCE is the remaining 16/25. The smaller triangle therefore has area 96 × 9/16 = 54 cm²; 96 is not the area of the original triangle.

questions.stem:
In a cuboid the base edges are in the ratio 3 : 4. The diagonal of the base equals the perpendicular height of the cuboid. The longest diagonal through the solid is 10√2 cm.

What is the volume of the cuboid?
questions.explanation: The two equal legs in the right triangle containing the solid diagonal must each be 10 cm. A base diagonal of 10 gives edges 6 cm and 8 cm by Pythagoras, so the volume is 6 × 8 × 10 = 480 cm³; 10√2 is not the height.

questions.stem:
A hollow cylindrical pipe has outer radius 5 cm, inner radius 3 cm and length 12 cm. The hole runs from end to end.

What is the total surface area of the pipe, including both ends and the inside wall?
questions.explanation: The two curved surfaces have total area 2π(5 + 3) × 12 = 192π cm². Both ring-shaped ends contribute 2π(5² − 3²) = 32π cm², giving 224π cm²; the ends are neither full discs nor a single ring.

questions.stem:
A pie chart represents 72 responses. The sector for ‘train’ is 145°.

How many responses were ‘train’?
questions.explanation: Each response accounts for 360° ÷ 72 = 5°, so 145° represents 29 responses. Dividing by 360 gives only the fraction of responses, not the count.

questions.stem:
A box contains only red, white and black beads. The probability of picking a red bead is 3/8. A white bead is twice as likely to be picked as a black bead.

What is the probability of picking a black bead?
questions.explanation: White and black share the remaining probability 5/8 in a 2 : 1 ratio, so black has probability (5/8) ÷ 3 = 5/24. Dividing by two would assume the two colours are equally likely.

questions.stem: A line of best fit on a scatter graph slopes downwards. All recorded x-values lie between 4 and 12. Which x-value could be used for interpolation?
questions.explanation: Interpolation estimates within the observed x-range, so 9 is the only possible choice. The negative slope does not make predictions outside the range interpolation.

questions.stem:
In a histogram, the interval 0 < t ≤ 4 has frequency 24. The bar for 4 < t ≤ 14 is half as high as that first bar.

What is the frequency for 4 < t ≤ 14?
questions.explanation: The first bar has frequency density 24 ÷ 4 = 6, so the second has density 3. Its width is 10, giving frequency 30; halving the height does not halve the frequency when the width changes.

questions.stem:
For a set of journey times, the median is 18 minutes and the interquartile range is 8 minutes. Each time is doubled and then increased by 5 minutes.

What are the new median and interquartile range, in minutes?
questions.explanation: The order is unchanged, so the median becomes 2 × 18 + 5 = 41. The 5-minute shift cancels in the difference between the quartiles, leaving an interquartile range of 2 × 8 = 16.

questions.stem: In 120 trials of a spinner, 18 results were green. Using the observed relative frequency, how many green results would you expect in the next 80 trials?
questions.explanation: The estimated probability is 18/120 = 3/20, giving 80 × 3/20 = 12 expected results. Reusing the count of 18 would ignore the change in the number of trials.

questions.stem:
Two fair spinners each have four sectors numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4. The two scores are multiplied.

What is the probability that the product is a multiple of 4?
questions.explanation: There are seven ordered pairs with at least one 4, plus (2, 2), so 8 of 16 pairs qualify. Counting only outcomes with a 4 misses (2, 2).

questions.stem:
A grouped frequency table has three classes of equal width, with midpoints 5, 15 and 25. Their frequencies are 6, k and 14 respectively. The estimated mean is 17.

What is k?
questions.explanation: The estimated mean is (6 × 5 + 15k + 14 × 25)/(20 + k), so 380 + 15k = 17(20 + k) and k = 20. Averaging the midpoints without weighting them ignores the class frequencies.

questions.stem:
Two machines make the same type of part. Machine A makes 60% of the parts and 1 in 10 of its parts is faulty. Machine B makes the rest and 1 in 5 of its parts is faulty.

A randomly chosen part is faulty. What is the probability it came from B?
questions.explanation: Out of 100 parts on average, A makes 6 faulty parts and B makes 8. Among the 14 faulty parts, 8 came from B, so the probability is 4/7; 1/5 is the probability of a fault given B, not the reverse.

questions.stem:
Of 45 pupils, 28 play football and 26 play tennis. At least 5 play neither sport.

What is the greatest possible number who play exactly one of the two sports?
questions.explanation: At most 40 play at least one sport, so at least 28 + 26 − 40 = 14 play both. With exactly 5 playing neither, exactly 26 can play just one (14 football only and 12 tennis only); counting all 40 would include the overlap.

questions.stem: What is the least positive integer divisible by both 14 and 30?
questions.explanation: The prime factors needed are 2, 3, 5 and 7, so their product is 210. Multiplying 14 by 30 counts the factor 2 twice.

questions.stem: A label gives an area of 2400 mm². What is its area in cm²?
questions.explanation: Each cm² measures 100 mm², so divide by 100, not 10.

questions.stem: Simplify √72 + √8.
questions.explanation: The terms are 6√2 and 2√2. Add their coefficients, not their radicands.

questions.stem:
A ribbon length x is recorded as 3.6 m to the nearest 0.1 m. Which statements are correct?

1. x could be 3.55 m.

2. x could be 3.65 m.

3. Two such ribbons could differ in length by 0.09 m.
questions.explanation: The interval is 3.55 ≤ x < 3.65. Lengths 3.55 and 3.64 differ by 0.09 m, but 3.65 rounds up.

questions.stem: Find the exact fraction for 0.2333…, with only the 3 recurring.
questions.explanation: Write it as 0.2 + 0.0333… = 1/5 + 1/30 = 7/30. The 2 is not in the repeating block.

questions.stem: A scale drawing is 1 : 250. A rectangular garden measures 8 cm by 6 cm on it. Which row gives its actual perimeter (m); area (m²)?
questions.explanation: The real sides are 20 m and 15 m. Their sum must be doubled for perimeter and multiplied for area.

questions.stem: A shop cuts a price by 30%, then raises the new price by 20%. What is the overall percentage change?
questions.explanation: The final multiplier is 0.7 × 1.2 = 0.84. Adding the percentages ignores the change in the base price.

questions.stem: Rain falls uniformly to a depth of 7.5 mm on a flat 24 m² roof. Four fifths reaches a tank initially holding 35 L. What volume is now in the tank, in litres?
questions.explanation: The roof receives 0.0075 × 24 = 0.18 m³, or 180 L. The tank gains 144 L, which must be added to the 35 L already in it.

questions.stem: A sensor logs 3 × 10⁵ values per hour, each using 4 × 10⁻³ MB. What is the storage for 15 minutes, in MB?
questions.explanation: An hour uses 1200 MB, and 15 minutes is a quarter of an hour, not 0.15 hours.

questions.stem: A machine’s rate is proportional to voltage squared and inversely proportional to resistance. Voltage rises by 50% and resistance rises by 25%. Find the new rate as a multiple of the original.
questions.explanation: The multiplier is (3/2)² ÷ (5/4) = 9/5. The resistance increase reduces the multiplier rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: Rearrange 5p − 2q = 3(p + r) to make p the subject.
questions.explanation: Subtract 3p and add 2q to obtain 2p = 2q + 3r. Divide both terms on the right by 2.

questions.stem: What is the constant term in (3x + 4)(2x − 5) + (x + 1)²?
questions.explanation: Set x = 0 to isolate the constant: 4(−5) + 1 = −19. Terms containing x contribute nothing.

questions.stem: The nth term of a sequence is 7 − 4n. Which is its first negative term?
questions.explanation: The first term is 3 and the next is −1. The first negative term is a value, not its position 2.

questions.stem: A line passes through (−2, 7) and (4, −5). Which row gives its gradient; its y-intercept?
questions.explanation: The change in y over the change in x is −12/6 = −2. Substituting (−2, 7) into y = −2x + c gives c = 3, not 11.

questions.stem: For x ≠ −4, simplify (x² + x − 12)/(x + 4).
questions.explanation: The numerator is (x + 4)(x − 3). Cancel the common factor, not individual terms.

questions.stem:
Which statements follow from −2 < x ≤ 3?

1. x + 4 > 2.

2. −x ≥ −3.

3. x² ≤ 4.
questions.explanation: Adding preserves order, so x + 4 > 2. Negating reverses the upper bound, and x = 3 disproves statement 3.

questions.stem: A quadratic sequence begins 2, 8, 18, 32. Find the difference between its ninth and tenth terms, taking the tenth minus the ninth.
questions.explanation: The terms are 2n², so the difference is 200 − 162 = 38. The second difference 4 measures how successive gaps change.

questions.stem: The graph y = (x + 1)(x − 7) crosses the x-axis twice. Which row gives the x-coordinate of the turning point; its y-coordinate?
questions.explanation: The turning point lies midway between the roots −1 and 7. Substitution at x = 3 gives 4 × (−4) = −16.

questions.stem: Let f(x) = 2x − 3 and g(x) = (x − 2)². The solutions of f(g(x)) = 15 are a and b. Find their product.
questions.explanation: First solve g(x) = 9, then x − 2 = ±3. The roots are −1 and 5; taking only the positive square root loses one.

questions.stem: A venue sells 44 tickets at two prices. Adult tickets cost £9 and child tickets £5. Total takings are £312. How many more adult than child tickets were sold?
questions.explanation: If all tickets cost £5, takings would be £220. The £92 difference buys 23 upgrades, leaving 21 child tickets and a difference of 2.

questions.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon measures 24°. How many sides does it have?
questions.explanation: The exterior angles sum to 360°, so divide 360 by 24. The number of degrees in one angle is not the number of sides.

questions.stem: A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. What is the sine of the angle opposite the other leg?
questions.explanation: The other leg is √(169 − 25) = 12. For the requested angle the opposite side is 12, not 5.

questions.stem: An arc has length 5π cm on a circle of radius 12 cm. Find its central angle in degrees.
questions.explanation: The arc is 5/24 of the circumference, so the angle is 5/24 of 360°. Using diameter in place of radius doubles the circumference if used in 2πr.

questions.stem:
Point (2, −5) is reflected in the y-axis, then translated 3 units right and 4 up. Which statements are correct?

1. Its distance from the origin is √2.

2. The final x-coordinate is 1.

3. The final y-coordinate is 9.
questions.explanation: Reflection changes x to −2 but leaves y at −5. Translation gives (1, −1), at distance √2 from the origin.

questions.stem: AB is a diameter of a circle. C lies on the circle, with AC = 9 and BC = 12. Find the circle’s radius.
questions.explanation: Angle ACB is 90°, so AB = √(81 + 144) = 15. This is the diameter; halve it for the radius.

questions.stem: Lengths in solid S are 3/2 of the matching lengths in a similar solid T. Which row gives S:T area ratio; volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Area scales by the square of 3/2 and volume by its cube, so the length ratio itself is neither answer.

questions.stem: From a harbour, a boat travels due west. What is the three-figure bearing of the harbour from the boat?
questions.explanation: The harbour is due east of the boat. The bearing is measured clockwise from north, so it is 090°, the reverse of 270°.

questions.stem: A rectangular face of a cuboid measures 6 cm by 8 cm. Its space diagonal is 26 cm. Which row gives the third edge (cm); volume (cm³)?
questions.explanation: The face diagonal is 10 cm. The third edge is √(26² − 10²) = 24 cm, so the volume is 6 × 8 × 24 = 1152 cm³.

questions.stem: A = (−2, 3) and B = (10, 9). P divides AB internally in the ratio AP:PB = 2:1. If Q = (6, −1), find the length PQ.
questions.explanation: Two thirds of the way from A to B gives P = (6, 7). The x-coordinates agree, so the length is the difference in y-coordinates, 8.

questions.stem: An open cylindrical tin has diameter 10 cm and height twice its radius. Its outside, including the base, is painted. Find the painted area in cm².
questions.explanation: The curved area is 2π × 5 × 10 and the one base is 25π. There is no lid to add.

questions.stem: Six observations in ascending order are 4, 6, 6, 10, 14, 20. What is their median?
questions.explanation: The two central observations are 6 and 10. Their mean is 8; neither observation alone is the median.

questions.stem: A card is drawn from 20 numbered cards. Four numbers are multiples of 5. What is the probability the card is not a multiple of 5?
questions.explanation: There are 16 cards in the complement, so the probability is 16/20. The 4 cards are the event being excluded.

questions.stem: A scatter plot suggests a positive association between revision hours and marks. Which conclusion is justified?

options.label: A
options.text: Revision always raises a student's mark.

options.label: B
options.text: Every point lies on a line.

options.label: C
options.text: The least revision must give the lowest mark.

options.label: D
options.text: Larger revision times tend to accompany higher marks in the data.

options.label: E
options.text: Revision is the only factor that can affect marks.

questions.explanation: Association describes an overall pattern in these observations. It does not establish that changing revision hours will change a mark.

questions.stem:
A histogram uses frequency density. Bins of widths 5, 10 and 20 have heights 4, 3 and 1. Which statements are correct?

1. The total frequency is 70.

2. The first bin has most observations.

3. The first and last bins have equal frequencies.
questions.explanation: The areas give frequencies 20, 30 and 20. The tallest bin does not have the highest count because it is narrow.

questions.stem: Roll a fair six-sided die twice. What is the probability that the second score equals the first?
questions.explanation: For every first roll exactly one second roll matches. There are six matching pairs out of 36, not one.

questions.stem: Two samples have sizes 8 and 12 and means 15 and 20 respectively. Which row gives the combined sum; the combined mean?
questions.explanation: Their sums are 120 and 240. Divide the combined sum by 20, rather than averaging the two means equally.

questions.stem: In a group of 36, 16 speak French, 14 speak Spanish and 9 speak neither. How many speak both?
questions.explanation: There are 27 in the union. Adding 16 and 14 counts bilingual members twice, so subtract 27 to obtain 3.

questions.stem: A box contains 5 blue and 3 yellow counters. Draw two without replacement. Which row gives the probability of two yellows; exactly one yellow?
questions.explanation: Two yellows have probability (3/8)(2/7). Exactly one yellow occurs in either order, with probability 2(3/8)(5/7); the second denominator is 7.

questions.stem: A list of ten values has mean 21. Two entries, 12 and 30, are replaced by 18 and x. The new mean is 22.5. Find x.
questions.explanation: The total rises by 15. Replacing 12 with 18 adds 6, so replacing 30 with x must add 9.

questions.stem: Three distinct codes are sampled uniformly without replacement from labels 1 to 6. What is the probability that the smallest selected label is 3?
questions.explanation: With 3 included, choose two from 4, 5 and 6, giving three sets. There are 20 equally likely three-element sets overall; ordering the codes is unnecessary.

questions.stem:
A current transfers 36 C through a wire in 45 s.

What is the current?
questions.explanation: Current is charge per unit time, so I = 36/45 = 0.80 A. Dividing time by charge gives the reciprocal.

questions.stem:
A student wants the current through a resistor and the potential difference across it.

How should the ammeter and voltmeter be connected relative to the resistor?

options.label: A
options.text: Ammeter in parallel; voltmeter in series

options.label: D
options.text: Ammeter in series; voltmeter not connected

options.label: E
options.text: Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel

options.label: F
options.text: Ammeter not connected; voltmeter in parallel

questions.explanation: All the resistor current must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in series. The voltmeter compares the potentials at the two ends, so it goes in parallel; swapping them changes what the meters measure.

questions.stem:
An electromagnet is used to pick up steel washers. Its core should lose most of its magnetism when the current is switched off.

Which property should its core have?

options.label: A
options.text: It should not be capable of magnetisation.

options.label: D
options.text: It should retain most of its magnetism.

options.label: E
options.text: It should be a permanent magnet.

questions.explanation: A magnetically soft core is easily magnetised and demagnetised. A magnetically hard material retains its magnetism and could keep hold of the washers.

questions.stem:
Two fixed resistors are connected in parallel across an ideal 12 V supply. One resistor is 8 Ω and the total current is 2.0 A.

What is the resistance of the other resistor?
questions.explanation: The 8 Ω branch takes 12/8 = 1.5 A, leaving 0.5 A in the other branch. That branch has the full 12 V across it, giving 24 Ω; the two currents need not be equal.

questions.stem:
A bar magnet is pushed north-pole-first into a stationary coil, producing a voltage pulse. It is then pulled back out along the same path at a greater speed.

Compared with the first pulse, what is true of the second?

options.label: A
options.text: Same polarity and greater peak magnitude

options.label: B
options.text: Opposite polarity and greater peak magnitude

options.label: C
options.text: Same polarity and lower peak magnitude

options.label: D
options.text: Opposite polarity and lower peak magnitude

options.label: F
options.text: Opposite polarity and the same peak magnitude

questions.explanation: Pulling the magnet out reverses the change in magnetic field through the coil, reversing the polarity. Faster motion makes the field change faster, so the peak magnitude increases; the same magnet does not imply the same voltage.

questions.stem:
Two heaters are each connected to the same ideal supply. Heater X has twice the resistance of heater Y and is switched on for three times as long.

What is the ratio of the energy transferred by X to that by Y?
questions.explanation: At fixed voltage, P = V²/R, so X transfers energy at half the rate of Y. It runs for three times as long, giving 3 : 2; using P = I²R with a fixed current would be wrong here.

questions.stem:
A negatively charged metal sphere is connected to Earth by a conducting wire. No other charged objects are nearby.

What happens as the sphere is discharged?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal numbers of protons and electrons leave the sphere.

options.label: B
options.text: Electrons flow from Earth to the sphere.

options.label: C
options.text: Protons flow from the sphere to Earth.

options.label: D
options.text: Protons flow from Earth to the sphere.

options.label: E
options.text: Electrons remain on the sphere because it is metal.

options.label: F
options.text: Electrons flow from the sphere to Earth.

questions.explanation: The sphere has excess electrons, which can move through the wire to Earth. The positive nuclei are not the mobile charge carriers in the metal.

questions.stem:
A straight wire carries 2.0 A perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. A second setup has an in-field length 50% greater than the first and one quarter of the original magnetic flux density. The wire is again perpendicular to the field.

What current gives 1.5 times the original magnetic force?
questions.explanation: With F = BIL, the 1.5 factor in length already provides the required 1.5 factor in force. The current must therefore be four times as large to offset the quarter-strength field, giving 8.0 A; increasing only the current by 50% would not compensate for the weaker field.

questions.stem:
A transformer supplies 1.8 kW at 120 V to a resistive load. Its input power is 2.4 kW at 480 V.

What is the ratio of the output current to the input current?
questions.explanation: The output current is 1800/120 = 15 A and the input current is 2400/480 = 5 A, so the ratio is 3 : 1. The 4 : 1 voltage ratio would give the current ratio only if no power were lost.

questions.stem:
A 6 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω resistors. The circuit is connected to an ideal 18 V supply. One resistor in the parallel pair is then disconnected while the other remains connected.

How does the power in the series resistor change?

options.label: A
options.text: It rises from 24 W to 54 W.

options.label: B
options.text: It falls from 24 W to 18 W.

options.label: C
options.text: It falls from 54 W to 24 W.

options.label: D
options.text: It falls from 24 W to 13.5 W.

options.label: F
options.text: It rises from 13.5 W to 24 W.

questions.explanation: Initially the total resistance is 9 Ω, so the series resistor carries 2 A and dissipates 24 W. After disconnection the total is 12 Ω, so it carries 1.5 A and dissipates 13.5 W; the supply voltage is fixed, not the current.

questions.stem:
A walker travels 60 m east in 20 s, then 20 m west in 10 s.

What is the walker’s average velocity for the whole trip?
questions.explanation: The net displacement is 40 m east in 30 s, giving 4/3 m/s east. Using the total distance of 80 m instead would give the average speed.

questions.stem:
A person pushes a wall horizontally with a force of 80 N. The wall does not move.

Which force forms a Newton’s third-law pair with this push?

options.label: A
options.text: An 80 N force by the wall on itself, opposite to the push

options.label: B
options.text: An 80 N force by the wall on the person, in the direction of the push

options.label: C
options.text: An 80 N force by the person on the wall, opposite to the push

options.label: D
options.text: An 80 N force by the wall on the person, opposite to the push

options.label: E
options.text: A 40 N force by the wall on the person, opposite to the push

options.label: F
options.text: No force, since the wall remains still

questions.explanation: The partner acts on the other object: the wall pushes the person with an equal and opposite force. The wall staying still concerns the net force on the wall, not this third-law pair.

questions.stem:
A motor lifts a 15 kg load vertically through 2 m in 5 s at constant speed. Take g = 10 m/s².

What useful power is delivered to the load?
questions.explanation: The useful energy gained is mgh = 15 × 10 × 2 = 300 J. Divide by 5 s to get 60 W; 300 is the energy in joules, not the power.

questions.stem:
A cyclist is moving at 6 m/s when the route begins to slope downwards. After travelling 20 m down the slope at constant acceleration, the cyclist is moving at 10 m/s.

What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation: Use v² − u² = 2as: a = (100 − 36)/40 = 1.6 m/s². The numerator is the difference of squares, not the square of the change in speed.

questions.stem:
A spring obeys Hooke’s law throughout an experiment. It takes 0.16 J of work to stretch it from its natural length to an extension of 2 cm.

How much additional work is needed to increase its extension from 2 cm to 4 cm?
questions.explanation: The stored energy scales as x², so at 4 cm it is 4 × 0.16 = 0.64 J. Subtract the energy already stored to get 0.48 J; 0.64 J is the total from the natural length.

questions.stem:
A 12 kg box slides down a vertical guide. The guide exerts an upward friction force of 84 N, and no other vertical force acts apart from weight. Take g = 10 m/s².

What is the box’s acceleration?
questions.explanation: The weight is 120 N, leaving a downward resultant of 120 − 84 = 36 N. Dividing by the mass gives 3.0 m/s² downwards; using only the friction would give the wrong resultant.

questions.stem:
A machine receives 900 J in one cycle. It transfers 180 J as unwanted heat and 90 J as unwanted sound. All remaining energy is useful.

What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation: The useful output is 900 − 180 − 90 = 630 J, so its efficiency is 630/900 = 70%. Only subtracting the heat would incorrectly treat the sound as useful.

questions.stem:
On a smooth track, a 0.40 kg cart moving right at 5 m/s collides with a 0.60 kg cart moving left at 2 m/s. After the collision, the first cart moves left at 1 m/s.

What is the final velocity of the second cart?
questions.explanation: Taking right as positive, the initial momentum is 2.0 − 1.2 = 0.8 kg m/s. The first cart ends with −0.4 kg m/s, so the second has +1.2 kg m/s, or 2 m/s right; subtracting unsigned speeds would lose the directions.

questions.stem:
A 2 kg trolley starts with speed 6 m/s at the foot of a ramp. By the time it reaches the top its speed is 2 m/s, and friction has transferred 12 J as heat. Take g = 10 m/s².

What is the vertical rise?
questions.explanation: The trolley loses ½ × 2 × (36 − 4) = 32 J of kinetic energy. After the 12 J dissipated, 20 J becomes gravitational potential energy, so h = 20/(2 × 10) = 1.0 m; assigning all 32 J to the climb ignores friction.

questions.stem:
A cart moving in a straight line has velocity +6 m/s at time 0 and −2 m/s at time 8 s. Its acceleration is constant throughout.

What total distance does it travel in those 8 s?
questions.explanation: The gradient is −1 m/s², so the cart reverses at 6 s. The two areas have magnitudes ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 m and ½ × 2 × 2 = 2 m; subtracting would give displacement rather than distance.

questions.stem:
Two identical metal plates have the same initial temperature, higher than their surroundings. One is matt black and the other polished silver. Only radiation transfers energy from the plates.

Which plate initially loses energy faster, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The silver plate, because it is the better infrared emitter.

options.label: B
options.text: The black plate, because it reflects more infrared radiation.

options.label: C
options.text: The black plate, because it is the better infrared emitter.

options.label: D
options.text: The silver plate, because it conducts thermal energy faster.

options.label: E
options.text: Neither, because the plates have the same temperature.

options.label: F
options.text: Neither, because infrared requires a material medium.

questions.explanation: A matt black surface emits infrared more effectively than a polished one at the same temperature and cools faster here. Conduction cannot explain the difference when only radiation transfers energy.

questions.stem:
A closed syringe contains air. Its plunger is pushed in, reducing the volume without any air escaping.

What happens to the average separation and the total number of air molecules?

options.label: C
options.text: Separation stays the same; number decreases.

options.label: D
options.text: Separation decreases; number stays the same.

options.label: E
options.text: Separation increases; number stays the same.

options.label: F
options.text: Separation stays the same; number stays the same.

questions.explanation: The same molecules now occupy a smaller volume, so their average separation decreases. Compression does not remove molecules from the sealed syringe.

questions.stem:
A metal sample has mass 84 g. When fully immersed in a measuring cylinder it raises the reading from 35 cm³ to 45 cm³.

What is the sample’s density?
questions.explanation: The displaced volume is 45 − 35 = 10 cm³, so density is 84/10 = 8.4 g/cm³. The final cylinder reading includes the original water volume.

questions.stem:
In a tank, water warmed by one wall rises along that wall. Water is always above 10 °C.

What completes the convection current?

options.label: A
options.text: Cooler, denser water rises and returns along the top.

options.label: B
options.text: Warmer, denser water sinks along the heated wall.

options.label: C
options.text: Water particles carry energy upward without any overall flow.

options.label: D
options.text: Cooler water at the bottom stays there and no water replaces the rising water.

options.label: E
options.text: Cooler, denser water sinks elsewhere and returns along the bottom.

options.label: F
options.text: The water sinks by the heated wall because pressure increases there.

questions.explanation: Warming decreases the density of the water here, so it rises. Cooler, denser water sinks elsewhere and flows back along the bottom; convection involves a bulk flow, not just energy passing between particles.

questions.stem:
A 600 W heater warms 0.50 kg of a liquid by 24 °C in 60 s. Half the energy supplied by the heater enters the liquid.

What is the liquid’s specific heat capacity?
questions.explanation: The liquid receives ½ × 600 × 60 = 18 000 J. Dividing by 0.50 × 24 gives 1500 J/(kg °C); 3000 assumes all the heater’s energy enters the liquid.

questions.stem:
A column of water of density 1000 kg/m³ is replaced in an open tube by a column of oil of density 800 kg/m³. Take g = 10 m/s².

If the water height was 0.40 m, what oil height gives the same pressure at the base?
questions.explanation: Both columns have the same atmospheric pressure above them, so match the values of ρgh. The oil must reach (1000/800) × 0.40 = 0.50 m; a less dense liquid needs a taller column, not a shorter one.

questions.stem:
A fixed mass of gas is in a sealed, frictionless syringe whose barrel has a uniform cross-sectional area. Its absolute pressure is 120 kPa when the gas column is 15 cm long.

What is the absolute pressure when the column is shortened to 10 cm at constant temperature?
questions.explanation: Volume is proportional to column length, so at constant temperature 120 × 15 = P × 10. Thus P = 180 kPa; treating the pressure as directly proportional to length reverses the change.

questions.stem:
A 0.30 kg block at 100 °C is placed in 0.20 kg of water at 20 °C. They reach 40 °C. Neglect energy transfer to the surroundings or container. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg °C).

What is the specific heat capacity of the block?
questions.explanation: The water gains 0.20 × 4200 × 20 = 16 800 J and the block loses that amount while cooling by 60 °C. Divide by 0.30 × 60 to get 2800/3 J/(kg °C); the temperature changes are not equal.

questions.stem:
A 300 W heater delivers all its energy to 0.20 kg of ice, initially at −10 °C. The specific heat capacity of ice is 2100 J/(kg °C) and its specific latent heat of fusion is 330 000 J/kg. The ice melts at 0 °C.

How long does it take for all the ice to become water at 0 °C?
questions.explanation: Warming the ice takes 4200 J and melting it takes a further 66 000 J. At 300 J/s this takes 70 200/300 = 234 s; 220 s accounts only for melting.

questions.stem:
A solid block of density 750 kg/m³ rests flat on the bottom of an empty tank. Its base area is 0.20 m². In a separate experiment, 0.30 m of water of density 1000 kg/m³ produces the same pressure above atmospheric at the bottom of the tank. Take g = 10 m/s².

What is the block’s mass?
questions.explanation: The water produces a gauge pressure of 3000 Pa. Multiplying by 0.20 m² gives a block weight of 600 N, hence mass 60 kg; the block density is not needed once the pressure and contact area are known.

questions.stem:
The period of a wave produced by a vibrating rod is 0.025 s.

What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is the reciprocal of period, so 1/0.025 = 40 Hz. The period itself specifies seconds per cycle, not cycles per second.

questions.stem:
An isotope has atomic number 17 and mass number 37.

How many neutrons does one nucleus contain?
questions.explanation: The mass number counts protons and neutrons together. Subtract the 17 protons to get 20 neutrons; 37 is not a neutron count.

questions.stem: Which radiation is not deflected as it passes between oppositely charged parallel plates?
questions.explanation: Gamma radiation has no electric charge and is not deflected. Alpha particles carry positive charge and beta-minus particles carry negative charge, so both are deflected but in opposite directions.

questions.stem:
Straight wavefronts in a ripple tank cross a boundary at an angle and travel faster in the new region.

What happens to the wavelength and frequency?

options.label: D
options.text: Wavelength decreases; frequency stays the same.

options.label: E
options.text: Wavelength stays the same; frequency increases.

options.label: F
options.text: Wavelength increases; frequency stays the same.

questions.explanation: The source fixes the frequency on both sides. With v = fλ, the higher speed therefore gives a longer wavelength; changing wave speed does not require a change in frequency.

questions.stem:
A moving ambulance passes a stationary observer who hears its siren. The ambulance moves at constant speed and emits a constant frequency.

How do the frequencies heard just before and just after it passes compare?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher before, equal to the emitted frequency after

options.label: B
options.text: Lower before, higher after, relative to the emitted frequency

options.label: C
options.text: Higher both before and after than the emitted frequency

options.label: D
options.text: Lower both before and after than the emitted frequency

options.label: E
options.text: Equal to the emitted frequency at both times

options.label: F
options.text: Higher before, lower after, relative to the emitted frequency

questions.explanation: The approaching source crowds the wavefronts and raises the received frequency. When it recedes the wavefronts spread out and the received frequency falls below the emitted one; it is pitch, not necessarily loudness, that identifies the Doppler shift.

questions.stem:
Two electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum. Wave X has twice the wavelength of wave Y.

What are the ratios X : Y for their speeds and frequencies, respectively?
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in vacuum. Since f = v/λ, X has half the frequency of Y; having a longer wavelength does not make it travel faster.

questions.stem:
A nucleus has mass number 218 and atomic number 84. It emits one alpha particle, then one gamma photon.

What are its final mass number and atomic number, respectively?
questions.explanation: Alpha emission removes two protons and two neutrons, giving 214 and 82. Gamma emission removes energy, not nucleons or charge, so the numbers do not change again.

questions.stem:
A sound wave of wavelength 0.40 m travels in air at 320 m/s, then enters a medium where its speed is 1.6 km/s.

How far does a compression travel in the new medium during three periods?
questions.explanation: The frequency is 320/0.40 = 800 Hz and stays fixed at the boundary. In the second medium the wavelength is 1600/800 = 2.0 m, so the compression moves 6.0 m in three periods; 1.2 m uses the air wavelength.

questions.stem:
A detector records 180 counts per minute from a sample plus background at time zero. It records 60 counts per minute 12 hours later. Background contributes a constant 20 counts per minute.

What is the sample’s half-life?
questions.explanation: Subtract the background to obtain sample rates of 160 and 40 counts per minute. The rate has halved twice in 12 hours, so the half-life is 6 h; use the corrected rates, not 180 and 60.

questions.stem:
Two plane mirrors have perpendicular reflecting surfaces. A light ray reflects from each mirror in turn, with both reflections in a plane perpendicular to the line where the mirrors meet.

What is the angle between the ray’s original and final directions of travel?

options.label: F
options.text: It depends on the angle at the first mirror.

questions.explanation: Each reflection reverses the velocity component perpendicular to that mirror. The perpendicular mirrors reverse the two perpendicular components in the ray’s plane, leaving the ray travelling in the opposite direction; 90° describes the mirrors, not the net turn.

questions.stem: A trolley slows uniformly from 14 m/s to 6 m/s in 4 s. Give its acceleration in m/s².
questions.explanation: Acceleration is (6 − 14)/4. A positive value would indicate an increase in velocity along the chosen axis.

questions.stem: A 4 kg box on a level floor is pulled right by 18 N and pushed left by 6 N. Friction is negligible. Find its acceleration.
questions.explanation: The net force is 12 N right. Dividing by 4 kg gives 3 m/s²; the forces oppose rather than add.

questions.stem: A lift moves upwards at 2 m/s for 9 s. How far does it rise?
questions.explanation: Multiply constant speed by time. Dividing time by speed does not give a distance.

questions.stem:
A lift is moving upwards but slowing. Consider a standing passenger, neglecting air resistance. Which statements are correct?

1. The passenger accelerates downwards.

2. The floor pushes up with less force than the passenger’s weight.

3. The two forces acting on the passenger form a Newton’s third-law pair.
questions.explanation: The resultant force is downwards, so the upward contact force is smaller than weight. These forces act on the same person and cannot be a third-law pair.

questions.stem: A robot travels north 18 m in 3 s, waits 2 s and travels south 8 m in 5 s. Which row gives average speed; magnitude of average velocity, both in m/s?
questions.explanation: Distance is 26 m and displacement is 10 m north. Divide both by 10 s, including the wait.

questions.stem: A 2 kg hanging mass descends with acceleration 3 m/s² on a taut vertical cord. Use g = 10 m/s². What is the cord tension?
questions.explanation: Weight is 20 N and the downward resultant is 6 N. Tension acts upwards, so it is 20 − 6 N.

questions.stem: A cart speeds up uniformly from rest to 8 m/s in 4 s and then slows uniformly to rest in 6 s. Which row gives total distance (m); average speed (m/s)?
questions.explanation: The area under the speed–time graph is ½ × 8 × 10 = 40 m. Average speed uses the whole 10 s rather than just the acceleration time.

questions.stem: Two blocks, 2 kg and 6 kg, touch on a frictionless table. A 24 N force pushes on the 2 kg block towards the 6 kg block. Which row gives acceleration (m/s²); contact force between blocks (N)?
questions.explanation: Both blocks share acceleration 24/8 = 3. The force accelerating the 6 kg block is 6 × 3 = 18 N, not the whole applied force.

questions.stem: A cyclist at 12 m/s coasts for 2 s before braking uniformly to rest over the next 3 s. How far does the cyclist travel in those 5 s?
questions.explanation: Coasting covers 24 m. Braking covers 3 × 6 = 18 m because the average braking speed is 6 m/s, so the total is 42 m.

questions.stem: A horizontal force of 30 N pulls a 5 kg sled. Its speed rises from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s. What constant opposing force acts on it?
questions.explanation: The acceleration is 2 m/s² and the resultant force is 10 N. The applied force exceeds the resultant by 20 N.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.8 kg moves north at 5 m/s. Give its momentum.
questions.explanation: Momentum is mass times velocity, with the same direction as velocity. Kinetic energy instead depends on speed squared.

questions.stem: A hoist delivers 240 J of useful work in 8 s. What is its useful power?
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work, so divide 240 J by 8 s.

questions.stem: An ideal spring extends 3 cm under a 9 N load. Find its spring constant.
questions.explanation: Convert 3 cm to 0.03 m before calculating F/x. Using centimetres gives 3 N/cm, not 3 N/m.

questions.stem:
A 0.5 kg ball arrives at a wall moving east at 8 m/s and leaves west at 4 m/s. Which statements are correct?

1. Its kinetic energy decreases.

2. The impulse from the wall is eastwards.

3. Its momentum changes by 6 kg m/s west.
questions.explanation: Taking east as positive, momentum changes from 4 to −2 kg m/s. Its speed and kinetic energy fall, and the impulse points west, like the momentum change.

questions.stem: A spring of constant 200 N/m is stretched from its natural length by 0.10 m. Which row gives its final tension (N); stored energy (J)?
questions.explanation: The final tension is kx = 20 N. The force rises from zero, so the energy is ½ × 20 × 0.10, not 20 × 0.10.

questions.stem: A frictionless track carries a cart from rest through a vertical drop of 5 m. Use g = 10 m/s². Find the final speed.
questions.explanation: Equate mgh to mv²/2, so v² = 100. The mass cancels, and 100 is the squared speed.

questions.stem: A motor draws 400 W for 10 s and transfers 2600 J usefully. Which row gives its efficiency; energy wasted (J)?
questions.explanation: Input is 4000 J. Useful output is 65% of that input, and the 1400 J difference is wasted.

questions.stem: A 2 kg trolley at 7 m/s east couples to a 3 kg trolley at 2 m/s west. Which row gives their common velocity (east positive, m/s); total kinetic energy after coupling (J)?
questions.explanation: Momentum is 14 − 6 = 8 kg m/s, so their common velocity is 8/5. Their kinetic energy is ½ × 5 × (8/5)², not the initial energy.

questions.stem: A 3 kg box slides down a ramp, dropping 4 m vertically over a path of 10 m. It starts at rest and leaves at 6 m/s. Use g = 10 m/s². Find the constant opposing force.
questions.explanation: The box loses 120 J of gravitational energy and gains 54 J of kinetic energy. Friction does 66 J of work in magnitude over 10 m.

questions.stem: A 0.25 kg puck moving at 8 m/s receives a 3 N s impulse opposite to its motion. Which row gives its final velocity (original direction positive, m/s); change in kinetic energy (J)?
questions.explanation: Momentum changes from +2 to −1 kg m/s, so v = −4 m/s. The kinetic energy falls from 8 J to 2 J even though the velocity reverses.

questions.stem: A 9 V cell drives 0.3 A through a resistor. Find its resistance.
questions.explanation: Use R = V/I, not VI, which is the power.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.25 A flows for 2 minutes. How much charge passes?
questions.explanation: Convert 2 minutes to 120 seconds before multiplying by 0.25 A.

questions.stem: A heater rated at 60 W runs from its rated 12 V supply. What current does it draw?
questions.explanation: Rearrange P = VI to get 60/12. Multiplying the voltage and rated power would not give current.

questions.stem: A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across 12 V. Which row gives total current (A); power in the 6 Ω resistor (W)?
questions.explanation: Branch currents are 2 A and 4 A. The 6 Ω branch dissipates 12 V × 2 A, not the total power taken from the supply.

questions.stem:
Two resistors are in series with an ideal fixed-voltage source. One resistance is increased. Which statements are correct?

1. The circuit current decreases.

2. Voltage across the unchanged resistor decreases.

3. The total power drawn increases.
questions.explanation: Total resistance rises, lowering current. Both the unchanged resistor’s voltage IR and the supply power VI decrease.

questions.stem: A 2 Ω resistor is placed in series with two 8 Ω resistors in parallel. Find the total resistance.
questions.explanation: The parallel pair has effective resistance 4 Ω. Add the separate 2 Ω series resistor, rather than adding all three directly.

questions.stem: A 1.2 kW appliance is run for 25 minutes on each of four days. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. Find the total cost.
questions.explanation: The operating time is 100/60 hours, so the appliance uses 2 kWh. Multiply by 30p, not by a charge for 100 hours.

questions.stem: A 12 V ideal supply feeds a 2 Ω series resistor followed by parallel 3 Ω and 6 Ω branches. Which row gives the voltage across the parallel pair (V); current through the 3 Ω branch (A)?
questions.explanation: The pair is equivalent to 2 Ω, so it gets half the supply voltage. Each branch has the full 6 V across it, and the 3 Ω branch draws 2 A.

questions.stem: A 10 V source feeds a 3 Ω resistor in series with an unknown resistor. Power in the 3 Ω resistor is 12 W. Find the unknown resistance.
questions.explanation: P = I²R gives I = 2 A. The total resistance is 5 Ω, which includes the 3 Ω already given.

questions.stem: A 4 Ω resistor takes 0.5 A for 30 s and 1.5 A for 10 s. Which row gives total charge (C); thermal energy transferred (J)?
questions.explanation: Sum It over the two intervals to get 30 C. The energies are 0.5² × 4 × 30 and 1.5² × 4 × 10; the current must be squared separately for each interval.

sets.title: Fields, thermal physics, waves and nuclei

questions.stem: The magnetic field through a closed coil is held constant after being increased. What happens to the induced current once the field stops changing?

options.label: A
options.text: It remains at the value during the increase.

options.label: E
options.text: It becomes independent of the resistance.

questions.explanation: Induction requires a change in magnetic flux. A steady field through a stationary coil does not sustain the current.

questions.stem: A travelling sound wave has frequency 500 Hz and speed 340 m/s. Find its wavelength.
questions.explanation: Divide speed by frequency to obtain wavelength. Inverting the ratio would give waves per metre.

questions.stem: A liquid has mass 560 g and volume 700 cm³. Find its density in g/cm³.
questions.explanation: Density is mass over volume, so 560/700 = 0.8. A volume-over-mass calculation gives the reciprocal.

questions.stem:
Infrared and visible light travel through a vacuum. Which statements are correct?

1. They travel at the same speed.

2. Infrared has a lower frequency than visible light.

3. Infrared has a shorter wavelength than visible light.
questions.explanation: Both travel at the speed of light in vacuum. Infrared has lower frequency, so equal speed means longer rather than shorter wavelength.

questions.stem: Give all 8400 J from a heater to 0.5 kg of water with specific heat capacity 4200 J/(kg °C). How much does its temperature rise?
questions.explanation: Divide energy by mc = 2100 J/°C. Dividing by the heat capacity per kilogram without applying the mass gives 2 °C.

questions.stem: An isotope with mass number 131 and atomic number 53 undergoes one beta-minus decay. Which row gives the daughter’s mass number; atomic number?
questions.explanation: A neutron becomes a proton, so the mass number stays fixed and the proton number increases by one.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has 600 primary turns and 150 secondary turns. Its primary takes 0.5 A at 48 V. Which row gives secondary voltage (V); secondary current (A)?
questions.explanation: The turns ratio reduces voltage to a quarter. Equal input and output power requires four times the current, not one quarter.

questions.stem: A counter reads 92 counts/min with a source and 12 counts/min with the source removed. After 18 h the total reading is 22 counts/min. Find the half-life.
questions.explanation: The source alone drops from 80 to 10 counts/min, a factor of 8 or three halvings. Do not apply the halving rule to the background.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has pressure 90 kPa and volume 24 cm³. It expands to 36 cm³ and then contracts to 18 cm³. Which row gives the pressures after expansion; after contraction (kPa)?
questions.explanation: The product pV stays 90 × 24 at both stages. Use the respective volumes as divisors, rather than assuming pressure is proportional to volume.

questions.stem: A pulse reflects from a wall. A microphone beside the sender picks up the echo 0.12 s after emission. Sound travels at 330 m/s. The wall moves 3.3 m farther away before a second pulse is emitted. What is the second echo delay?
questions.explanation: The extra path is 6.6 m because the pulse travels out and back. This takes 0.02 s, so add that to the first delay.

questions.stem:
Three elements have atomic numbers 8, 9 and 10. Their most common isotopes have mass numbers 16, 19 and 20, respectively.

What determines the order of these elements in the Periodic Table?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of neutrons in an atom

options.label: B
options.text: The mass number of the most common isotope

options.label: C
options.text: The number of occupied electron shells

options.label: D
options.text: The number of protons in an atom

options.label: E
options.text: The number of electrons in the first shell

options.label: F
options.text: The sum of the protons, neutrons and electrons

questions.explanation: The Periodic Table orders elements by atomic number, which is the proton count. Even if mass numbers happen to increase in the same order in this example, they do not determine the position.

questions.stem:
Atom X has 12 protons and 12 neutrons.

Which atom is a different isotope of the same element as X?
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. A nucleus with 11 protons and 13 neutrons has the same mass number as X, but belongs to a different element.

questions.stem: Which feature best explains why neon is much less chemically reactive than sodium?

options.label: A
options.text: Neon has a full outer electron shell.

options.label: C
options.text: Neon has only one electron shell.

options.label: D
options.text: Neon has one electron in its outer shell.

options.label: E
options.text: Neon is less reactive because it has more protons than sodium.

options.label: F
options.text: Neon needs to gain one electron to fill its outer shell.

questions.explanation: Neon already has a full outer shell, so it has little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons. One electron in the outer shell describes sodium, not neon.

questions.stem:
Equal-sized pieces of lithium and potassium are compared in a reaction with excess water.

What is true of the more reactive metal and the gas produced?

options.label: A
options.text: Lithium is more reactive; both give hydrogen.

options.label: B
options.text: Potassium is more reactive; both give oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: Potassium is more reactive; both give hydrogen.

options.label: D
options.text: Lithium is more reactive; both give oxygen.

options.label: E
options.text: Potassium is more reactive; it gives hydrogen but lithium gives oxygen.

options.label: F
options.text: The metals are equally reactive; both give hydrogen.

questions.explanation: Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group, so potassium reacts more vigorously. Both metals form hydroxides and release hydrogen; the different rates do not imply different gases.

questions.stem:
Oxygen and aluminium have atomic numbers 8 and 13, respectively.

How many electrons are there in one O²⁻ ion and one Al³⁺ ion, respectively?
questions.explanation: Oxygen gains two electrons to form O²⁻, while aluminium loses three to form Al³⁺. Both then have ten electrons; a positive ion has lost electrons, not gained them.

questions.stem:
Solid carbon dioxide sublimes at a much lower temperature than is needed to break up the lattice of diamond.

Which statement explains this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Carbon dioxide molecules contain only weak covalent bonds, whereas diamond contains strong ones.

options.label: B
options.text: Diamond contains strong ionic bonds; carbon dioxide does not.

options.label: C
options.text: Only intermolecular forces are overcome in diamond, and they are weaker in carbon dioxide.

options.label: D
options.text: Diamond has large molecules held together by ionic bonds.

options.label: E
options.text: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken in diamond, but only intermolecular forces are overcome when solid carbon dioxide sublimes.

options.label: F
options.text: The molecules in solid carbon dioxide are held together by metallic bonds.

questions.explanation: Diamond is a giant covalent network, while solid carbon dioxide consists of separate molecules. Sublimation separates those molecules without breaking their strong C=O bonds.

questions.stem:
Iron is extracted from its oxide in the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.

Which statement describes the change to the iron compound?

options.label: A
options.text: It is oxidised because it loses oxygen.

options.label: B
options.text: It is reduced because it gains oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: It is oxidised because iron changes from +3 to 0.

options.label: D
options.text: It is neither oxidised nor reduced because the oxygen atoms are conserved.

options.label: E
options.text: It is reduced because it loses oxygen.

options.label: F
options.text: It is reduced because it loses electrons.

questions.explanation: The iron oxide loses oxygen and is reduced to iron. The oxygen atoms are still present in carbon dioxide, but atom conservation does not rule out redox.

questions.stem:
A compound contains only the ions T³⁺ and U²⁻. An identical set of ions occurs 12 times in a sample, each set being the smallest electrically neutral combination.

How many U²⁻ ions are in the sample?
questions.explanation: Two T³⁺ ions give +6 and three U²⁻ ions give −6. There are therefore 3 × 12 = 36 anions; the charge on an individual ion is not its count in a formula unit.

questions.stem:
Element J has electron configuration 2,8,2 and element K has electron configuration 2,7. J and K form an ionic compound in which both ions have full outer shells.

How many electrons are present in one formula unit of the compound?
questions.explanation: J loses two electrons to become J²⁺ and each K gains one to become K⁻. The formula is JK₂, with 10 electrons per ion, so there are 30 electrons; counting only one ion of each would give 20.

questions.stem:
Transition metal X forms XO and X₂O₃. Oxygen has oxidation state −2 in both.

For equal numbers of X atoms, what is the ratio of oxygen atoms in XO to those in X₂O₃, and how does X’s oxidation state change from XO to X₂O₃?
questions.explanation: Two XO units and one X₂O₃ unit each contain two metal atoms, but have two and three oxygen atoms respectively. Balancing the oxygen oxidation states gives +2 then +3 for X; comparing one unit of each would not use equal numbers of X atoms.

questions.stem:
What is the relative formula mass of magnesium phosphate, Mg₃(PO₄)₂?

Relative atomic masses: Mg = 24, P = 31, O = 16.
questions.explanation: There are three Mg, two P and eight O atoms per formula unit, so the relative formula mass is 72 + 62 + 128 = 262. The outer 2 multiplies everything inside the parentheses.

questions.stem: A student adds excess zinc to dilute hydrochloric acid. After removing the unreacted zinc, which salt remains in solution?
questions.explanation: A metal reacting with hydrochloric acid forms a chloride salt and hydrogen. Removing the leftover metal does not remove the dissolved zinc chloride.

questions.stem:
At the temperature and pressure used, one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³.

How many moles are in 360 cm³ of gas?
questions.explanation: Convert 360 cm³ to 0.360 dm³ and divide by 24 dm³/mol. Dividing 360 directly by 24 mixes cubic centimetres and cubic decimetres.

questions.stem:
A 50 cm³ sample of a 0.40 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solution is mixed with 150 cm³ of a 0.20 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solution. Assume the volumes add.

What is the resulting concentration?
questions.explanation: The solutions contribute 0.020 and 0.030 mol, giving 0.050 mol in 0.200 dm³. That is 0.25 mol/dm³; taking the simple mean ignores the unequal volumes.

questions.stem:
A hot saturated solution contains 48 g of a salt per 100 g of water. It is cooled without losing water until the solubility is 20 g per 100 g of water.

How much salt crystallises if the solution contains 150 g of water?
questions.explanation: In 150 g of water there are initially 72 g of dissolved salt and finally 30 g, so 42 g crystallises. The 28 g difference in the stated solubilities is per 100 g of water, not per 150 g.

questions.stem:
Acid solution A has pH 3 and acid solution B has pH 5.

What is the ratio of the hydrogen ion concentration in A to that in B?
questions.explanation: A drop of one pH unit means ten times the hydrogen ion concentration. A is two units lower, so its concentration is 100 times B’s; the higher pH is the less acidic solution.

questions.stem:
A mixture contains 0.20 mol of CO and 0.30 mol of CO₂.

Which fraction of the total mass is oxygen?

Relative atomic masses: C = 12, O = 16.
questions.explanation: There are 0.50 mol of carbon atoms and 0.80 mol of oxygen atoms, with masses 6.0 g and 12.8 g respectively. The mass fraction is 12.8/18.8 = 32/47; the fraction of atoms that are oxygen is not the mass fraction.

questions.stem:
Iron reacts with sulfur: Fe + S → FeS. A mixture of 14.0 g of iron and 6.4 g of sulfur reacts as completely as possible.

What total mass of solid is left, excluding the iron sulfide?

Relative atomic masses: Fe = 56, S = 32.
questions.explanation: The starting amounts are 0.25 mol Fe and 0.20 mol S. Sulfur limits the 1 : 1 reaction, leaving 0.05 mol of iron, or 2.8 g; a 1 : 1 mole ratio does not imply equal reacting masses.

questions.stem:
A 10 cm³ sample of nitric acid is diluted to 100 cm³. A 40 cm³ portion of the diluted acid is exactly neutralised by 15 cm³ of 0.016 mol/dm³ calcium hydroxide solution.

What was the nitric acid concentration before dilution?
questions.explanation: One mole of Ca(OH)₂ neutralises two moles of HNO₃, so the 40 cm³ portion contains 2 × 0.015 × 0.016 = 0.00048 mol of acid. This is 0.012 mol/dm³ after dilution, so the original concentration was ten times higher, 0.12 mol/dm³; using a 1 : 1 mole ratio would halve the answer.

questions.stem:
Magnesium carbonate decomposes: MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂. When 16.8 g of magnesium carbonate is used, 6.0 g of magnesium oxide is collected.

What is the percentage yield of magnesium oxide?

Relative atomic masses: Mg = 24, C = 12, O = 16.
questions.explanation: The 16.8 g sample is 0.20 mol of MgCO₃, so the theoretical yield is 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g of MgO. The yield is 6.0/8.0 = 75%; the starting carbonate mass is not the theoretical oxide yield.

questions.stem: Which state-symbol change represents solid sodium chloride dissolving in water?
questions.explanation: Solid is (s) and dissolved in water is (aq), so NaCl(s) → NaCl(aq) is the correct representation. The symbol (l) would mean liquid sodium chloride itself, not its solution.

questions.stem:
A reaction in an insulated cup makes the surrounding solution warmer. There is no external heating.

What is the sign of the enthalpy change of the reaction, and how is it classified?
questions.explanation: The reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so it is exothermic with negative ΔH. The solution warming does not mean that the reacting system gained enthalpy.

questions.stem: Why is direct current used rather than alternating current to maintain steady deposition of a metal at one electrode?

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the metal ions negatively charged.

options.label: C
options.text: It reverses the electrodes at regular intervals.

options.label: D
options.text: It keeps the same electrode negative.

options.label: E
options.text: It prevents ions from moving in the electrolyte.

options.label: F
options.text: It removes the need for an electrolyte.

questions.explanation: The negative electrode attracts metal cations and supplies electrons, so holding it negative keeps deposition at the same electrode. Alternating current reverses the electrode polarities.

questions.stem:
In a closed vessel, CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g). Raising the temperature decreases the amount of CO₂ at equilibrium.

What is the sign of ΔH for the forward reaction, and what would decreasing the volume at constant temperature do to the position of equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Heating favours the reverse direction, so the forward reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative. Compression would favour the side with fewer moles of gas, but there are two on each side, so there is no shift.

questions.stem:
A lump of an insoluble solid reacts with a solution. The experiment is repeated with the same mass of solid powdered instead, keeping the solution concentration and temperature fixed.

Why is the initial rate higher with the powder?

options.label: A
options.text: More surface is exposed, giving more collisions per second between the reactants.

options.label: B
options.text: Particles in the powder have higher average kinetic energy.

options.label: C
options.text: The powder lowers the reaction’s activation energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The powder increases the total number of solid particles at the atomic level.

options.label: E
options.text: The powder increases the solution’s concentration.

options.label: F
options.text: The powder increases the energy of each collision.

questions.explanation: Powdering exposes more of the solid to the solution, so more collisions can occur each second. It does not itself raise the temperature or lower the activation barrier.

questions.stem:
A reaction produces 12 cm³ of gas by 10 s and 21 cm³ by 25 s.

What is the average rate of gas production between 10 and 25 s?
questions.explanation: The volume increases by 9 cm³ in the 15 s interval, so the average rate is 0.60 cm³/s. Dividing 21 by 25 gives the average from the start, not for this interval.

questions.stem: In the ionic reaction 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, which species acts as the reducing agent?
questions.explanation: Iodide loses electrons to form iodine, so it is oxidised and reduces Fe³⁺. Fe³⁺ accepts the electrons and is the oxidising agent, not the reducing agent.

questions.stem:
The uncatalysed forward activation energy of a reversible reaction is 90 kJ/mol. The products are 20 kJ/mol above the reactants. A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy to 55 kJ/mol without changing the product or reactant energies.

What are the uncatalysed and catalysed activation energies, respectively, for the reverse reaction?
questions.explanation: The reverse reaction starts at the products, 20 kJ/mol above the reactants. The two peaks are 90 and 55 kJ/mol above the reactants, so the reverse barriers are 90 − 20 = 70 and 55 − 20 = 35 kJ/mol; the catalyst changes the peak, not the starting energy.

questions.stem:
Ethene reacts with hydrogen: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆. Use these mean bond energies, in kJ/mol: C=C 610, C–C 350, H–H 440, C–H 410.

What is the estimated enthalpy change per mole of ethene?
questions.explanation: The changed bonds are one C=C and one H–H broken, and one C–C and two C–H formed. The estimate is 610 + 440 − 350 − 2 × 410 = −120 kJ/mol; counting only one new C–H bond misses one added hydrogen.

questions.stem:
During electrolysis of molten magnesium chloride, the electrode products are magnesium metal and chlorine gas. Assume no side reactions.

Which pair gives the moles of magnesium atoms and chlorine molecules produced, respectively, when 0.60 mol of electrons passes through the external circuit?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg uses two electrons per metal atom, and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ releases two per chlorine molecule. Both amounts are 0.60/2 = 0.30 mol; the number of chlorine atoms would be twice the number of molecules.

questions.stem: What changes when pure liquid water freezes at its freezing point?

options.label: B
options.text: The molecules move freely past one another more easily.

options.label: C
options.text: The molecules become fixed in position but continue to vibrate.

options.label: E
options.text: The molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

options.label: F
options.text: The arrangement becomes less ordered and the molecules move much farther apart.

questions.explanation: In ice, the molecules vibrate about fixed positions instead of moving past one another as they do in a liquid. Freezing changes their arrangement and motion, not the identity of the molecules.

questions.stem: Why is chlorine added in controlled amounts during drinking-water treatment?

options.label: B
options.text: To supply fluoride for dental health

options.label: F
options.text: To soften the water by removing calcium ions

questions.explanation: Chlorine disinfects water by killing harmful microorganisms. Fluoride, where used, has a different purpose and does not explain chlorination.

questions.stem:
A salt containing just one type of metal ion gives a lilac flame in a flame test.

Which metal ion is indicated?
questions.explanation: Potassium gives a lilac flame. Sodium gives a yellow-orange flame, so a lilac colour does not indicate sodium.

questions.stem:
A mixture contains an insoluble solid and dissolved salt in water. A student wants to recover both solids separately, without needing to collect the water.

Which sequence works?

options.label: B
options.text: Crystallise first, then filter out both solids together.

options.label: C
options.text: Decant once, then dry what remains without further separation.

options.label: E
options.text: Use a separating funnel, then evaporate the lower layer.

options.label: F
options.text: Centrifuge once, then dry only the pellet.

questions.explanation: Filtration collects the insoluble solid as the residue. The dissolved salt passes into the filtrate, which can then be concentrated and crystallised; it will not be recovered by drying the residue alone.

questions.stem:
Hex-2-ene reacts with enough hydrogen to add across its carbon–carbon double bond. No carbon atoms are lost.

What is the product?
questions.explanation: Adding H₂ makes the double bond single and adds two H atoms to C₆H₁₂, giving C₆H₁₄. Hydrogenation neither shifts the double bond nor introduces oxygen.

questions.stem: What is the correct name of the alcohol CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has six carbon atoms, and numbering from the nearer end puts OH at carbon 3. Numbering from the other end gives 4, but the lower locant must be used.

questions.stem:
Two colourless solutions contain different sodium halides. After acidification with dilute nitric acid and addition of aqueous silver nitrate, solution X gives a cream precipitate and Y gives a yellow precipitate.

Which halides are present in X and Y, respectively?
questions.explanation: Silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow. Chloride would form a white precipitate, so it cannot account for either observation.

questions.stem:
On a chromatogram, the baseline is 10 mm from the bottom edge of the paper and the solvent front is 70 mm from that edge. A reference dye has an Rf of 0.60 in this solvent.

How far from the bottom edge would a spot with the same Rf be?
questions.explanation: The solvent travelled 60 mm from the baseline, so the spot travelled 0.60 × 60 = 36 mm from the same line. Add the 10 mm baseline offset; 36 mm is not the distance from the bottom edge.

questions.stem:
Propane burns in limited oxygen and produces carbon monoxide and water as its only products. The equation is balanced using the smallest whole-number coefficients.

What is the sum of all four coefficients?
questions.explanation: First write C₃H₈ + ⁷⁄₂O₂ → 3CO + 4H₂O, then double all coefficients to give 2, 7, 6 and 8, whose sum is 23. Treating the carbon product as CO₂ would require more oxygen.

questions.stem:
Propanoic acid, C₂H₅COOH, reacts with solid MgCO₃ to give a magnesium salt, carbon dioxide and water. The reaction produces 0.050 mol of carbon dioxide.

What mass of the magnesium salt forms?

Relative atomic masses: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, Mg = 24.
questions.explanation: The salt is Mg(C₂H₅COO)₂, with relative formula mass 24 + 2 × 73 = 170. Each mole of carbonate gives one mole of CO₂ and one mole of the salt, so 0.050 × 170 = 8.5 g; the 2 : 1 acid-to-salt ratio is not the CO₂-to-salt ratio.

questions.stem: A neutral aluminium atom has atomic number 13. How many electrons are in its outer shell in the ground state?
questions.explanation: Its arrangement is 2,8,3. Atomic number gives total electrons in the neutral atom, not just outer-shell electrons.

questions.stem: A main-group atom has electron arrangement 2,8,7. What is its period?
questions.explanation: Three shells are occupied. The seven outer electrons relate to the group rather than the period.

questions.stem: Why does pure solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?

options.label: B
options.text: Its electrons carry a net positive charge.

options.label: C
options.text: The sodium and chloride are neutral atoms.

questions.explanation: The ions are fixed in the solid lattice. When molten, the ions can move and carry charge without becoming neutral.

questions.stem:
Two neutral magnesium isotopes are ²⁴Mg and ²⁶Mg, both with atomic number 12. Which statements are correct?

1. Both have twelve electrons.

2. The heavier isotope has two more protons.

3. The heavier isotope has fourteen neutrons.
questions.explanation: The atomic number fixes proton number at 12 and hence the neutral electron count. Neutrons in ²⁶Mg number 26 − 12.

questions.stem: Which property is shared by atoms of neon and argon in their ground states?

options.label: A
options.text: They have the same number of occupied shells.

options.label: B
options.text: They each have two outer electrons.

options.label: C
options.text: They have the same atomic number.

questions.explanation: Both are noble gases with filled outer shells. Being in the same group does not give them the same number of occupied shells.

questions.stem: A compound contains only Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ ions. Which row gives the numbers of calcium ions; phosphate ions in its simplest formula unit?
questions.explanation: The smallest equal charge totals are +6 and −6, requiring three calcium and two phosphate ions. Subscripts do not equal the corresponding charge magnitudes directly.

questions.stem: Which particles primarily carry charge through a solid copper wire?

options.label: C
options.text: Copper ions moving along the wire

questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons can move through the metal. Copper ions remain in the lattice and do not drift along the wire.

questions.stem: An element contains only isotopes of mass numbers 63 and 65. Its relative atomic mass is 63.6. What percentage of atoms are the heavier isotope?
